final_answer:
No, the trial court most likely did not err. Texas law governs (Dallas state district court; answer as of 2026-10-02). I could not fetch the primary opinions: every opinion host I tried was blocked by the network proxy. The rules below come from search-result summaries of In re Columbia Valley Healthcare System, L.P., 320 S.W.3d 819 (Tex. 2010), and they are unverified against the opinion text. The answer is therefore lower confidence than the firewall standard requires.

1. Framework. Texas disqualifies a firm over a nonlawyer's prior work in two steps. First, a nonlawyer who worked on a matter for the former client is conclusively presumed to have acquired that client's confidences. Second, the presumption that the nonlawyer shared those confidences with the new firm is rebuttable, but only by showing that the firm (a) instructed her not to work on the matter and (b) took other reasonable steps to keep her off it. Even if screening was used, disqualification is required if the nonlawyer actually works on the same matter at the new firm's direction and the firm reasonably should have known of the conflict. In that case the presumption of shared confidences becomes conclusive (C1, C2; A1, unverified).

2. Application. Jones prepared litigation documents, took part in several hundred privileged communications and attended strategy meetings on the Apex v. Prestige suit. That satisfies step one. At Smith Fullingham she worked on the same matter on 13 occasions and e-filed two documents under her own name for the attorney. The firm made no inquiry when it hired her. It adopted no screen until Apex objected in 2023, years after she started working on the case. Her claimed lack of recall, and the firm's statement that she shared nothing, do not rebut the presumption. Once she actually worked on the matter at attorney direction, the presumption is conclusive. The firm should reasonably have known of the conflict, because the firm was counsel in the case and could have asked at hiring or checked her name against its matters. Because she worked on the matter directly, the later promise to screen her comes too late (C3).

3. Delay and waiver. Apex learned of Jones in January 2023 and moved in early March 2023, a delay of about two months. Texas treats waiver of a disqualification motion as requiring unreasonable delay, which is not apparent here. I did not verify the waiver authority, so this point is an unresolved caveat and not a cited proposition (C4).

Conclusion. Disqualification was proper under the Columbia Valley rule if that rule is as the summaries describe it. If review is by mandamus, the standard is abuse of discretion, which the trial court is unlikely to have exceeded.

claims.text: Texas applies a conclusive presumption that a nonlawyer who worked on the same matter for the former client acquired its confidences, and a rebuttable presumption that she shared them with the new firm.
If the nonlawyer actually works on the matter at the new firm's direction and the firm reasonably should know of the conflict, screening cannot save the firm and disqualification is required.
On these facts (13 occasions, 2 e-filings, no inquiry or screen until 2023) the trial court did not err.
A two-month delay is unlikely to amount to waiver; this was not verified.
